lessons.title: Verifying physician orders
body: Every procedure starts with a valid order: right patient, right test, right protocol, ordering provider, and any limitations or prep instructions.

If the order is unclear, conflicts with what the patient says, or a prep instruction was not followed (e.g., beta blocker not held), stop and clarify with the ordering provider. Never substitute or add a test on your own.
keyPoints: Check: patient, procedure, protocol, provider, reason, limitations
Verbal orders only in urgent situations, then documented per policy
Unable to exercise → physician may change to pharmacologic stress

mnemonics.name: The 5 Ps of an order
mnemonics.text: Patient, Procedure, Protocol, Provider, Precautions/limitations.

lessons.title: Patient identification & HIPAA
body: Use at least two identifiers (name + DOB or MRN) and compare them with the wristband and order. Ask open-ended: "Tell me your name and date of birth." Room numbers are never identifiers.
HIPAA protects patient health information. Share only with people involved in care; secure printouts and screens; patients request records through the facility process.
keyPoints: Room/bed number is NOT an identifier
Unknown patient → facility temporary ID system
Never discuss PHI in public areas
Label every tracing: name/ID, date, time

mnemonics.name: Two-ID rule
mnemonics.text: "Name and Date" before every touch.

lessons.title: Consent
body: Implied consent: the patient's actions show agreement (routine ECG). Informed consent: written, after the provider explains purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives (stress testing). A healthcare proxy decides when the patient lacks capacity. Emergency care proceeds under implied consent.
A competent adult can refuse or withdraw consent at any time—including mid-test. Stop, notify and document.
keyPoints: Patient request to stop = indication to stop exercise

mnemonics.name: Informed consent PRA
mnemonics.text: Purpose, Risks, Alternatives (+ benefits).

lessons.title: Infection control & isolation
body: Standard precautions for everyone: hand hygiene, gloves when contact with blood/body fluids is possible, clean equipment between patients. Transmission-based precautions add: contact (gown + gloves: MRSA, C. diff), droplet (surgical mask: influenza), airborne (N95 + negative-pressure room: TB, measles, varicella).
C. diff spores need soap and water. PPE on: gown → mask → goggles → gloves. PPE off: gloves → goggles → gown → mask, then hand hygiene.
keyPoints: Airborne: N95 + negative pressure (TB, measles, chickenpox)

mnemonics.name: Airborne "MTV"
mnemonics.text: Measles, TB, Varicella → N95.

mnemonics.name: Donning order
mnemonics.text: Gown, Mask, Goggles, Gloves — "Go Make Good Gains"; take off in alphabetical order: Gloves, Goggles, Gown, Mask.

lessons.title: Transfer, transport & body mechanics
body: Lock wheelchair/stretcher brakes, lower the bed, use a gait belt, bend at the knees and keep the load close. Patients with one-sided weakness transfer toward their strong side.
Transport with side rails up, feet first, never leave the patient unattended. Monitored patients travel with staff qualified per policy.
keyPoints: Lift with legs, not back; no twisting

lessons.title: Anatomical landmarks & lead placement
body: Find the angle of Louis → 2nd rib → count down to the 4th intercostal space. V1 right sternal border, V2 left sternal border, V4 5th ICS midclavicular line, V3 midway V2–V4, V5 anterior axillary line and V6 midaxillary line level with V4.
Place chest electrodes under (not on) breast tissue. Right-sided: V4R mirrors V4. Posterior: V7 posterior axillary, V8 tip of scapula, V9 paraspinal, level with V6.
keyPoints: V1: 4th ICS RSB · V2: 4th ICS LSB
V4: 5th ICS MCL · V3: between V2 and V4
V5: AAL · V6: MAL (level with V4)
V7 PAL · V8 scapula tip · V9 paraspinal

mnemonics.text: V1 and V2 in the 4th space, V4 in the 5th.

mnemonics.name: Limb colors (AHA)
mnemonics.text: "White on right, smoke (black) over fire (red), snow (white) over grass (green)" — RA white, LA black, LL red, RL green.

lessons.title: Patient preparation & skin prep
body: Position supine and relaxed (semi-Fowler's if dyspneic, and note it). Skin prep: clip hair, clean oils/lotion, dry completely, lightly abrade for stress/Holter, then apply fresh, moist electrodes from the same manufacturer.
Keep the patient warm and covered, explain the test, and ask them to lie still and breathe normally—most artifact is prevented before you press "record".
keyPoints: Remove lotion; clip, clean, dry, abrade

mnemonics.name: Skin prep "CCDA"
mnemonics.text: Clip, Clean, Dry, Abrade.

lessons.title: Equipment calibration & maintenance
body: Standard settings: 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, diagnostic filter 0.05–150 Hz. Half standard = 5 mm/mV, double = 20 mm/mV; always show calibration on the tracing. At 50 mm/s each small box = 0.02 s.
Remove damaged cables from service, keep inspection stickers current (biomed), and clean equipment with approved disinfectants. Stress labs must check the defibrillator and crash cart.
keyPoints: Small box 0.04 s · large box 0.20 s
Diagnostic filter 0.05–150 Hz; monitor 0.5–40 Hz distorts ST

lessons.title: Patient & environmental safety
body: Electrical safety: grounded three-prong plugs, no damaged cords, no liquids on carts; patients with pacing wires or central lines are vulnerable to microshock. Prevent falls (rails, bed low, stay with confused patients).
Emergencies: unresponsive and not breathing normally → call for help, start CPR (100–120/min, ≥2 in deep), get the AED. Vasovagal fainting → lay flat, elevate legs, monitor.
keyPoints: Microshock risk with direct cardiac conductors
Treat the patient, not the monitor

mnemonics.name: Emergency C-A-B
mnemonics.text: Compressions, Airway, Breathing.

lessons.title: Patient education
body: Explain purpose, procedure, what the patient will feel and what you need from them, in plain language; check understanding. Use qualified interpreters.

You do not interpret results for the patient—"Your physician will review it with you." Give prep instructions (shoes, caffeine, medications per physician) for stress tests and diary/water instructions for Holters.
keyPoints: ECG is painless; no electricity is delivered
Do not interpret results to the patient
Stress: walking shoes, follow medication instructions, report symptoms

lessons.title: ECG supplies & color codes
body: A 12-lead uses 10 electrodes (4 limb + 6 chest) to produce 12 leads. RL is a ground/reference.
AHA colors: RA white, LA black, LL red, RL green; V1 red, V2 yellow, V3 green, V4 blue, V5 orange, V6 purple. IEC: RA red, LA yellow, LL green, RL black.
keyPoints: AHA limb: white, black, red, green
AHA chest: red, yellow, green, blue, orange, purple

mnemonics.name: Chest colors
mnemonics.text: "Roy G. Bop" order: Red, Yellow, Green, Blue, Orange, Purple for V1–V6.

lessons.title: Lead systems & Einthoven
body: Bipolar limb leads: I (RA− → LA+, 0°), II (RA− → LL+, +60°), III (LA− → LL+, +120°). Augmented unipolar: aVR (−150°), aVL (−30°), aVF (+90°). Precordial V1–V6 view the horizontal plane.
Einthoven's law: I + III = II. Current toward a positive electrode is upright; away is downward; perpendicular is biphasic. Perpendicular pairs: I–aVF, II–aVL, III–aVR.
keyPoints: Hexaxial: I 0°, II +60°, III +120°, aVF +90°, aVL −30°, aVR −150°

lessons.title: ECG paper & calibration
body: At 25 mm/s: 1 small box = 0.04 s, 1 large box = 0.20 s, 5 large boxes = 1 s, 30 large boxes = 6 s. At 10 mm/mV: 1 small box = 0.1 mV.
Half standard (5 mm/mV) halves heights; double standard (20 mm/mV) doubles them. At 50 mm/s every small box = 0.02 s and complexes look twice as wide.

lessons.title: Artifact & troubleshooting
body: Somatic tremor: irregular jittery baseline (cold, anxious, Parkinson) → warm, relax, support limbs, move limb electrodes proximally. Wandering baseline: slow drift (breathing, lotion, cable tension) → re-prep, secure wires. 60-cycle: uniform fine regular fuzz → unplug devices, check grounding and cable routing. Loose lead: flat or erratic in one lead → reattach.
Lead reversal: LA/RA → lead I inverted, aVR upright. Always check the patient first, then electrodes → wires → machine → environment.
keyPoints: Only one lead abnormal → technical problem
Inverted I + upright aVR → arm leads reversed

mnemonics.name: Troubleshoot P-E-W-M-E
mnemonics.text: Patient, Electrodes, Wires, Machine, Environment.

lessons.title: Performing the 12-lead
body: Order + two identifiers → explain/consent → supine, skin prep → limb electrodes, then V1, V2, V4, V3, V5, V6 → enter age/sex → record 10 s → check quality (all leads, labels, calibration) → remove and clean.
Chest pain during the ECG: finish quickly and hand it to the nurse/physician immediately. Computer statements are not final interpretations.
keyPoints: Check tracing quality before removing electrodes

lessons.title: Modified ECGs
body: Right-sided leads (V3R/V4R) for RV infarction and pediatrics; posterior V7–V9 for posterior MI; 15-lead = 12 + V4R, V8, V9. Dextrocardia: reverse arm electrodes and mirror the chest leads on the right. Always relabel modified tracings.
Lewis lead enhances atrial activity; MCL1 approximates V1 for monitoring.
keyPoints: Dextrocardia: reverse arms + right-sided chest leads

lessons.title: Cardiac A&P for the ECG
body: Blood flow: venae cavae → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonic → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → aorta. Layers: endocardium, myocardium, epicardium, pericardium.

Conduction: SA node (60–100) → atria → AV node (delay; junction 40–60) → His → bundle branches → Purkinje (20–40). CO = HR × SV. Coronaries fill in diastole. RCA: inferior wall, SA & AV nodes (most people); LAD: anterior wall & septum; circumflex: lateral wall.
keyPoints: P = atrial depol · QRS = ventricular depol · T = ventricular repol
RCA → inferior; LAD → anterior/septal; LCx → lateral

mnemonics.name: Valve order
mnemonics.text: "Try Pulling My Aorta": Tricuspid, Pulmonic, Mitral, Aortic.

lessons.title: Electrical axis
body: Normal −30° to +90°. Quadrant method: lead I and aVF both positive → normal. I positive, aVF negative → check II: II positive = normal (0 to −30°), II negative = left axis deviation. I negative, aVF positive → right axis deviation. Both negative → extreme axis.
Find the most equiphasic limb lead; the axis is perpendicular to it, toward the positive lead. Causes: LAD—LAFB, inferior MI, LVH; RAD—RVH, COPD, PE, LPFB, normal newborn.
keyPoints: Thumbs: I & aVF both up = normal

mnemonics.name: Two thumbs
mnemonics.text: Left thumb = lead I, right thumb = aVF. Both up = normal; "reaching" toward each other (I up, aVF down) = Left; "leaving" (I down, aVF up) = Right.

lessons.title: Bundle branch blocks
body: Complete BBB: QRS ≥ 0.12 s. RBBB: rSR' ("rabbit ears") in V1–V2, wide S in I and V6. LBBB: deep QS/rS in V1, broad notched R without q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6, discordant ST-T.
Use V1 as the "turn signal": terminal deflection up = right, down = left. New LBBB with chest pain is reported urgently.
keyPoints: RBBB: rSR' in V1, wide S in I/V6
LBBB: QS in V1, broad R in V6, no septal q

mnemonics.name: WiLLiaM MaRRoW
mnemonics.text: LBBB: W in V1, M in V6. RBBB: M in V1, W in V6.

lessons.title: Chamber enlargement & hypertrophy
body: LVH (Sokolow-Lyon): S V1 + R V5/V6 ≥ 35 mm; strain = lateral ST depression/T inversion. RVH: R ≥ S in V1, right axis. Right atrial enlargement: tall P ≥ 2.5 mm in II (P pulmonale). Left atrial enlargement: broad notched P ≥ 0.12 s (P mitrale), deep terminal negative P in V1.
Check calibration before applying voltage criteria; young thin adults can have high voltage normally.
keyPoints: RVH: tall R in V1 + RAD
P pulmonale (RAE) tall; P mitrale (LAE) wide/notched

lessons.title: Ischemia, injury & infarction by lead group
body: Lead groups: Inferior II, III, aVF (RCA). Septal V1–V2 and anterior V3–V4 (LAD). Lateral I, aVL, V5–V6 (circumflex). Posterior: mirror changes in V1–V3 (tall R, ST depression); confirm with V7–V9. RV: V4R.

Ischemia: ST depression/T inversion. Injury: ST elevation (≥1 mm in two contiguous leads; V2–V3 ≥2 mm men ≥40, ≥2.5 mm men <40, ≥1.5 mm women). Necrosis: pathologic Q (≥0.04 s or ≥25% of R). Evolution: hyperacute T → ST elevation → Q → T inversion. Reciprocal depression supports STEMI. Electrolytes: high K peaked T; low K U waves; high Ca short QT; low Ca long QT.
keyPoints: Measure ST at the J point vs baseline

mnemonics.name: I SAW LA
mnemonics.text: Inferior: II, III, aVF · Septal: V1–V2 · Anterior: V3–V4 · Lateral: I, aVL, V5–V6.

lessons.title: Stress test supplies
body: Multi-lead stress ECG system, electrodes and skin prep (abrasion), BP cuff, treadmill or cycle, consent, and a checked defibrillator with emergency drugs and airway equipment.
Limb electrodes go on the torso (Mason-Likar); record supine and standing baselines. Secure cables to limit motion artifact.

lessons.title: Treadmill & cycle ergometer
body: Treadmill workload = speed + grade; cycle workload = watts. Cycle peak VO2 is usually lower (local leg fatigue). Handrail gripping overestimates capacity. 1 MET = 3.5 mL O2/kg/min.
Teach safe on/off technique; know the emergency stop; calibrate equipment regularly.
keyPoints: Bike in watts; treadmill in mph/% grade

lessons.title: Protocols, heart rate & BP response
body: Bruce (3-min stages): 1.7/10 → 2.5/12 → 3.4/14 → 4.2/16 → 5.0/18 (mph/% grade). Modified Bruce adds 1.7/0 and 1.7/5 first. Naughton/Balke/ramp use small increments. Aim for 8–12 minutes.
APMHR = 220 − age; target ≥ 85%. SBP rises with workload; DBP stable. Double product = HR × SBP. Positive ECG: ≥1 mm horizontal/downsloping ST depression 60–80 ms after J. Monitor recovery ≥5–6 min.

lessons.title: Contraindications to exercise testing
body: Absolute: acute MI within 2 days, ongoing unstable angina, uncontrolled symptomatic arrhythmia, symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, decompensated heart failure, acute PE, acute myocarditis/pericarditis, acute aortic dissection.

Relative: left main stenosis, moderate stenotic valve disease, electrolyte abnormalities, severe resting hypertension (>200/110), tachy/bradyarrhythmias, high-degree AV block, HCM with obstruction, inability to exercise adequately.

mnemonics.name: Absolute "MUD PAMS"
mnemonics.text: MI (≤2 d), Unstable angina, Dissection, PE, Arrhythmia (uncontrolled), Myocarditis/pericarditis, Stenosis (severe symptomatic AS) — plus decompensated HF.

lessons.title: When to stop the test
body: Absolute: ST elevation >1 mm in leads without Q waves (not V1/aVR); SBP drop >10 mm Hg with other ischemia signs; moderate–severe angina; CNS symptoms (ataxia, dizziness, near-syncope); poor perfusion (pallor, cyanosis); sustained VT; can't monitor ECG/BP; patient asks to stop.

Relative: >2 mm horizontal/downsloping ST depression, SBP drop without ischemia signs, increasing chest pain, fatigue/SOB/claudication, non-sustained arrhythmias (multifocal PVCs, triplets, SVT, block), hypertensive response (>250/115), BBB indistinguishable from VT.
keyPoints: ST elevation = absolute; >2 mm depression = relative

lessons.title: Pharmacologic & nuclear stress
body: Vasodilators: adenosine, regadenoson (0.4 mg bolus), dipyridamole—hold caffeine 12–24 h; reversal agent aminophylline; caution in active bronchospasm. Dobutamine raises HR/contractility in 3-min stages (+/− atropine); reverse with a short-acting beta blocker.

Nuclear perfusion tracers (e.g., Tc-99m sestamibi) are injected at peak stress; stress defect that normalizes at rest = reversible ischemia; fixed defect = scar. LBBB/paced patients → vasodilator stress.

lessons.title: Stress test patient care
body: Explain the test, teach symptom reporting, stay close to the patient and the stop button, and monitor ECG/BP continuously. Use Borg (effort) and angina scales.
Emergencies (VF, collapse): call code, CPR, defibrillate. Observe until stable before discharge; advise against hot showers right afterward.
keyPoints: Discharge only when stable and cleared

lessons.title: Types of ambulatory monitoring
body: Holter: continuous 24–48 h. Event/loop recorder: up to ~30 days, patient- or auto-triggered with pre-event memory. Mobile cardiac telemetry: auto-transmits events. Patch: single-lead, days–2 weeks. Implantable loop recorder: up to ~3 years. Telemetry: in-hospital central monitoring.
Match the device to symptom frequency: daily → Holter; weekly/monthly → event/MCT; rare → ILR.

lessons.title: Holter equipment checks
body: Before: charged/new battery, correct time/date, intact lead wires, memory cleared. After application: verify a clean signal on each channel. On return: confirm full recording, collect diary, clean/disinfect.
keyPoints: Verify signal before the patient leaves

lessons.title: Holter hook-up
body: Prep skin thoroughly (clip, clean, dry, abrade). Place electrodes over bone (sternum, ribs), avoid large muscles and breast tissue. Make stress (strain-relief) loops and tape them; secure the recorder in a pouch.

lessons.title: Holter patient education
body: Keep the device dry (no showers/baths/swimming), continue normal activities, log symptoms and activities with times, press the event button if available, re-press a loose electrode and note it, and avoid electric blankets/strong magnetic fields. A Holter is not an alarm—call 911 for emergencies.

lessons.title: Holter troubleshooting
body: Flat line in one channel → loose electrode/broken wire. Short recording → battery/memory or early removal. Activity-related noise → motion/muscle artifact that can mimic VT. Wandering baseline → poor prep or movement.

lessons.title: Holter analysis basics
body: Reports include min/max/average HR, ectopy counts, pauses, arrhythmia episodes, and diary correlation. Sinus bradycardia during sleep is common. Pauses ≥3 s are usually flagged. A symptom with normal rhythm is also useful information.

lessons.title: Waves, intervals & QTc
body: P = atrial depolarization (≤0.12 s). PR 0.12–0.20 s (start P → start QRS). QRS < 0.12 s (usually 0.06–0.10). QT from QRS start to T end; QTc = QT/√RR (Bazett), prolonged ≥0.45 s men/≥0.46 s women; >0.50 s high risk. ST segment J point → T start.
Measure intervals in the lead where they are longest and clearest; count small boxes × 0.04 s.

mnemonics.name: Box math
mnemonics.text: "Small 4, Large 20" — 0.04 s and 0.20 s.

lessons.title: Calculating heart rate
body: Regular rhythm: 300 ÷ large boxes between R waves (300-150-100-75-60-50) or 1,500 ÷ small boxes (most precise). Irregular rhythm: QRS count in 6 seconds × 10. Rate from R–R in seconds: 60 ÷ R–R.
Atrial rate: use P–P (or flutter-wave) intervals the same way.

lessons.title: Sinus rhythms
body: All sinus rhythms: upright P in II before every QRS, constant PR 0.12–0.20 s, narrow QRS. NSR 60–100; sinus bradycardia <60; sinus tachycardia >100; sinus arrhythmia: R–R varies ≥0.16 s with breathing; sinus arrest/pause: missing P–QRS–T, not an exact multiple of the P–P.
keyPoints: Pause not a multiple of P–P = arrest

lessons.title: Atrial rhythms
body: PAC: early, different P, narrow QRS, non-compensatory pause. Atrial fibrillation: no P waves, irregularly irregular. Atrial flutter: sawtooth F waves ~300/min with 2:1, 3:1, 4:1 block (2:1 flutter often ≈150 bpm). SVT: regular narrow tachycardia 150–250, P hidden. MAT: ≥3 P shapes, rate >100, irregular; WAP: same but <100.

mnemonics.name: Irregularly irregular
mnemonics.text: If you can't find a pattern and can't find P waves → AF.

lessons.title: Junctional rhythms
body: Impulses from the AV junction: narrow QRS; P inverted in II with PR <0.12 s, hidden in the QRS, or after the QRS. Junctional escape 40–60, accelerated junctional 60–100, junctional tachycardia >100. PJC: early junctional beat.
keyPoints: Inverted P/short PR, hidden, or after

mnemonics.name: Junction "before, during, after"
mnemonics.text: P before (short PR), during (hidden), or after the QRS — all inverted.

lessons.title: Ventricular rhythms
body: PVC: early, wide (≥0.12 s), bizarre, no P, T opposite, full compensatory pause. Bigeminy every other beat; trigeminy every third; couplet two in a row; ≥3 = VT. Multifocal = different shapes. VT: wide, regular, >100. Torsades: twisting polymorphic VT (long QT). VF: chaotic, no output. Asystole: flat line—confirm in two leads. Idioventricular 20–40; accelerated idioventricular 40–100.
keyPoints: PVC: wide, early, no P, compensatory pause

mnemonics.name: Shockable?
mnemonics.text: "Shock the V's": VF and pulseless VT. Asystole and PEA → CPR + epinephrine.

lessons.title: AV heart blocks
body: 1st degree: PR >0.20 s, constant, every P conducted. 2nd degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach): PR lengthens until a P is dropped—grouped beating. Mobitz II: constant PR, sudden dropped QRS, often wide QRS, dangerous. 2:1 block: every other P dropped (type can't be determined). 3rd degree: P and QRS independent; atrial rate > ventricular; escape junctional (narrow 40–60) or ventricular (wide 20–40).
keyPoints: Mobitz II: constant PR, sudden drop

mnemonics.name: Wenckebach poem
mnemonics.text: "Longer, longer, longer, drop — then you have a Wenckebach."

mnemonics.name: Mobitz II
mnemonics.text: "If some P's don't get through, then you have a Mobitz II."

mnemonics.name: 3rd degree
mnemonics.text: "If P's and Q's don't agree, then you have a third degree."

lessons.title: Bundle branch block on rhythm strips
body: On a monitoring lead (V1/MCL1), RBBB shows rSR'; LBBB shows a deep wide QS. QRS ≥0.12 s with a P before every QRS = sinus rhythm with BBB (not VT).
keyPoints: Sinus + wide QRS + P before each = BBB

lessons.title: Pacemaker rhythms & malfunction
body: Atrial pacing: spike → P. Ventricular pacing: spike → wide QRS. Dual-chamber: both spikes. NBG code: chamber paced, chamber sensed, response (VVI, DDD…). Failure to capture: spike without a following complex. Failure to sense (undersensing): spikes fire despite intrinsic beats (risk of spike on T). Oversensing: inappropriate inhibition → pauses without spikes.
keyPoints: Spike + no complex = failure to capture
No spike when expected = oversensing/failure to pace
VVI: paces V, senses V, inhibited

mnemonics.name: NBG letters
mnemonics.text: "Paced, Sensed, Response" — PSR.

lessons.title: Recognizing artifact on strips
body: Artifact does not interrupt the real rhythm: look for QRS complexes continuing on time. Tremor = irregular jitter (can mimic AF/flutter); 60-cycle = uniform fine oscillation; wandering baseline = slow drift; loose lead = sudden erratic/flat segment in one lead.
keyPoints: Check the patient before calling VF/asystole

lessons.title: Life-threatening rhythms
body: VF, pulseless VT, torsades, asystole and PEA are cardiac arrest. VF/pVT: CPR + defibrillation. Asystole/PEA: CPR + epinephrine (no shock). Mobitz II and 3rd-degree block can cause sudden severe bradycardia → notify immediately, pacing may be needed. Always confirm with the patient (pulse, responsiveness).
keyPoints: Asystole → CPR + epinephrine, confirm in 2 leads

lessons.title: Reporting rhythm findings
body: Report critical rhythms immediately using closed-loop communication (identify, state finding, read-back). Label strips with patient ID, date/time and lead. Do not interpret to the patient—refer to the provider.

lessons.title: Cardiac medications & the ECG
body: Beta blockers (-olol, class II): ↓HR, ↑PR. Non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil, class IV): ↓HR/AV conduction. Class III (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide): ↑QT. Class I (procainamide, flecainide, lidocaine): Na-channel block, ↑QRS. Digoxin: scooped ST, short QT; toxicity → many arrhythmias (worse with low K). ACE inhibitors (-pril): cough, ↑K. ARBs (-sartan). Loop diuretics: ↓K → U waves.

ACLS: adenosine (SVT, rapid push + flush), atropine (symptomatic bradycardia), epinephrine (arrest), amiodarone/lidocaine (VF/pVT), magnesium (torsades). Stress: aminophylline reverses vasodilators; beta blocker reverses dobutamine.
keyPoints: -olol beta blocker · -pril ACE-I · -sartan ARB · -dipine DHP CCB
Class I Na · II β · III K (QT↑) · IV Ca
Digoxin: scooped ST; toxicity ↑ with low K
Adenosine → SVT; atropine → brady; epi → arrest

mnemonics.name: Vaughan Williams "Some Block Potassium Channels"
mnemonics.text: I Sodium, II Beta, III Potassium, IV Calcium.

lessons.title: How to read each lead group
body: Read a 12-lead in the same order every time: rate → rhythm → intervals (PR, QRS, QT) → axis → hypertrophy → then look at each lead group for Q waves, ST changes and T waves.

INFERIOR (II, III, aVF): look up from the diaphragm at the inferior LV wall — RCA in most people. ST elevation here: check aVL/I for reciprocal depression and record V4R for RV involvement. Watch for bradycardia/AV block.
SEPTAL (V1, V2): the septum — LAD. Normal: small r, deep S. ST depression with tall R here may be the mirror of a posterior MI.
ANTERIOR (V3, V4): anterior LV wall — LAD. R waves should be growing; the R/S transition is usually here.
LATERAL (I, aVL high lateral; V5, V6 low lateral): lateral LV wall — circumflex (or diagonal branches of the LAD). Small septal q waves are normal here.
aVR: looks at the heart from the right shoulder; normally everything is negative. An upright aVR with inverted lead I suggests arm-lead reversal.
POSTERIOR: no standard lead — look for ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3 and confirm with V7–V9.

mnemonics.name: I SAW LA
mnemonics.text: Inferior II/III/aVF, Septal V1–V2, Anterior V3–V4, Lateral I/aVL/V5–V6.

lessons.title: A 5-step method for any rhythm strip
body: 1. Rate: regular → 1500 ÷ small boxes (or 300 ÷ large boxes); irregular → QRS in 6 s × 10. Check atrial rate too.
2. Regularity: march out R–R intervals with calipers or paper; regular, regularly irregular (grouped), or irregularly irregular?
3. P waves: present? upright in II? one before every QRS? more P waves than QRS complexes? flutter or fibrillatory waves?
4. PR interval: 0.12–0.20 s? constant, lengthening, or variable (dissociated)?
5. QRS: narrow (< 0.12 s, supraventricular) or wide (ventricular, BBB, paced)? Then name the rhythm and look for ectopy, pauses and pacing spikes.
keyPoints: More P than QRS = AV block

mnemonics.name: Rate, Rhythm, P, PR, QRS
mnemonics.text: "Real Rhythm Pros Prefer QRS."

lessons.title: Chambers, valves & heart wall
body: Four chambers: two thin-walled atria receive blood; two ventricles pump it. The right atrium receives the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus. The left atrium receives four pulmonary veins. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps to the whole body.

Valves keep flow one-way. Atrioventricular valves: tricuspid (right, 3 cusps) and mitral/bicuspid (left, 2 cusps), held by chordae tendineae and papillary muscles. Semilunar valves: pulmonic and aortic (3 cusps each, no chordae).
Heart sounds: S1 "lub" = AV valves close at the start of systole (just after the QRS). S2 "dub" = semilunar valves close at the start of diastole (near the end of the T wave).

Wall layers inside → out: endocardium, myocardium, epicardium (visceral pericardium), then pericardial fluid, parietal pericardium and fibrous pericardium. The heart sits in the mediastinum; the apex is at about the left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
keyPoints: S1 = AV close, S2 = semilunar close

mnemonics.name: Valve order
mnemonics.text: "Try Pulling My Aorta": Tricuspid, Pulmonic, Mitral, Aortic.

mnemonics.name: Left side has the "L" valves
mnemonics.text: LAB: Left Atrioventricular = Bicuspid (mitral). Tricuspid is on the right ("Tri before you Bi").

lessons.title: The full path of blood
body: Right heart (deoxygenated): superior & inferior venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonic valve → pulmonary artery → lungs.
Left heart (oxygenated): lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta.
Systemic circuit: aorta → arteries → arterioles (resistance, BP control) → capillaries (gas exchange) → venules → veins (valves, low pressure, reservoir) → venae cavae.

Exceptions to remember: the pulmonary ARTERY carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary VEINS carry oxygenated blood. "Artery" means away from the heart, not "oxygenated". The first branches of the aorta are the coronary arteries.

Fetal shunts: the foramen ovale (RA → LA) and ductus arteriosus (pulmonary artery → aorta) bypass the lungs and close after birth. Failure: left heart → backs up into lungs (dyspnea); right heart → backs up into body veins (edema, liver).
keyPoints: Body → VC → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonic → PA → lungs
Lungs → PV → LA → mitral → LV → aortic → aorta

mnemonics.name: Right side sequence
mnemonics.text: "Very Red Tomatoes Rarely Pop Pretty" — Vena cava, Right atrium, Tricuspid, Right ventricle, Pulmonic valve, Pulmonary artery.

mnemonics.name: Arteries go Away
mnemonics.text: A for Artery, A for Away from the heart — regardless of oxygen.

lessons.title: Coronary arteries & territories
body: The right and left coronary arteries leave the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve and fill mainly during diastole.
Left main → LAD (anterior wall, apex, most of the septum; leads V1–V4) and circumflex (lateral wall; leads I, aVL, V5–V6). A left main lesion threatens most of the LV.
RCA (most people): right ventricle (V4R), inferior LV wall (II, III, aVF), SA node in most people and the AV node in most people. That is why inferior MIs often bring bradycardia and AV block.
Dominance = which artery gives the posterior descending artery (PDA); right dominance is most common. Venous blood drains into the coronary sinus → right atrium.
keyPoints: RCA → II, III, aVF (inferior) + RV + SA/AV nodes

mnemonics.name: RCA "rules the rate"
mnemonics.text: The RCA usually feeds the SA and AV nodes, so inferior MI → watch for slow rates and blocks.

lessons.title: The conduction system
body: SA node (high RA, near the SVC; 60–100/min) → atria (internodal pathways; Bachmann bundle to the LA) → AV node (low interatrial septum near the coronary sinus; built-in delay so the atria can finish emptying) → bundle of His → right bundle branch and left bundle branch (left anterior and left posterior fascicles) → Purkinje fibers (fastest conduction).
Back-up pacemakers: AV junction 40–60/min, ventricles 20–40/min. A slower site takes over only if faster sites fail ("escape").
Septal depolarization goes left → right from early left-bundle fibers: that makes the small r in V1 and the small septal q waves in I, aVL, V5–V6 (lost in LBBB).
Properties of cardiac cells: automaticity (fires on its own), excitability (responds to a stimulus), conductivity (passes it on), contractility (shortens).
keyPoints: SA → atria → AV → His → BBs → Purkinje

mnemonics.name: Conduction order
mnemonics.text: "Sally Always Arrives Before Breakfast, Pancakes" — SA, Atria, AV node, Bundle of His, Bundle branches, Purkinje.
SA 60–100, junction 40–60, ventricle 20–40.

lessons.title: Cardiac cycle & hemodynamics
body: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (≈ 5 L/min at rest). Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume. Ejection fraction = SV ÷ EDV (normal LVEF roughly 50–70%).

Preload = filling stretch at end-diastole; afterload = resistance to ejection; contractility = strength at a given stretch. Frank-Starling: more stretch → stronger beat (within limits). Atrial kick adds roughly the last 20–30% of filling and is lost in atrial fibrillation.

Cycle: atrial systole (after the P wave) → AV valves close (S1) → isovolumetric contraction (all valves closed) → ejection (semilunar valves open, ST segment/T wave time) → semilunar valves close (S2) → isovolumetric relaxation → passive filling.
Control: sympathetic (norepinephrine, beta-1) ↑ rate and force; parasympathetic (vagus, acetylcholine) ↓ SA rate and AV conduction. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch adjust both.

lessons.title: Action potential & refractory periods
body: Ventricular action potential: phase 0 rapid sodium influx (QRS) → phase 1 early repolarization → phase 2 plateau, calcium in / potassium out (ST segment) → phase 3 repolarization, potassium out (T wave) → phase 4 resting potential (set mainly by potassium).

Absolute refractory period: from the QRS to about the peak of the T wave; no stimulus can trigger another beat. Relative refractory (vulnerable) period: the downslope of the T wave; a strong stimulus here (R-on-T PVC, unsynchronized shock) can start VT/VF.
Atrial repolarization is usually hidden in the QRS. A wide QRS means the impulse crawled through muscle instead of the Purkinje system.

lessons.title: Patient communication & dignity
body: Every encounter: knock, introduce yourself (name and role), confirm identity with two identifiers, explain the test in plain words (what they will feel, how long, what to do), and ask permission. Close the curtain and drape — expose only what you need.

Barriers: hearing loss → face the patient, quiet room, write it down. Language → qualified medical interpreter (not children or untrained relatives except in emergencies). Anxiety → acknowledge, explain each step, tell them they can tell you to stop. Pain or limited mobility → modify position and document it; lock brakes and assess before transfers.

Rights: a competent adult may refuse any procedure. Listen, explain the purpose, and if they still refuse, do not proceed — notify the nurse/provider and document. HIPAA: share information only with the patient or people they authorize; never discuss results in hallways.
Scope: technicians do not interpret results for patients. Say the physician will review the tracing and discuss it. Use teach-back ("Tell me in your own words…") to confirm understanding.
Upset or angry patients: stay calm, listen, acknowledge feelings, apologize for delays, explain next steps. If you feel unsafe, step away and get help.
keyPoints: Right to refuse: stop, notify, document

mnemonics.name: AIDET
mnemonics.text: Acknowledge, Introduce, Duration, Explanation, Thank you — a common patient-communication framework.

lessons.title: Recognizing a deteriorating patient
body: Warning signs: new chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion or decreased responsiveness, pale/cool/sweaty skin, fainting or near-fainting, sudden rhythm change, very low or very high blood pressure.

What to do: stay with the patient, keep them safe (lie them down, prevent falls), call for help (nurse, rapid response or code per policy), and give the team the facts you observed. Never leave a possibly unstable patient alone to find help.

If unresponsive and not breathing normally: call for help, check pulse for no more than 10 seconds, start CPR and get the defibrillator/AED. A strange-looking rhythm on the monitor: check the PATIENT first — a talking patient with "VF" has artifact.
keyPoints: Check the patient, not just the monitor
Stay, keep safe, call for help
Report facts: time, symptoms, rhythm, BP

lessons.title: Documentation
body: Document objectively: date/time, what was done, any modification (position, torso limb leads, right-sided or posterior leads), patient symptoms, and who was notified.
Refusals: record that the purpose was explained, the patient's reason, and whom you told. Never record a test as done when it was not.
Errors in demographics are corrected through the facility process before transmission; do not overwrite printed tracings or delete records.
